Explain the factors that control the rate of decomposition

say.en: Every year a forest drops tonnes of leaves, yet the floor never fills up. Earthworms, fungi and bacteria break them down and return the nutrients to the soil. In this lesson: Define detritus and decomposition.
Describe the five steps of decomposition.
Explain the factors that control the rate of decomposition.

body.en: Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide, water and nutrients; this process is called decomposition. Dead plant remains such as leaves, bark and flowers, and dead remains of animals including faecal matter, constitute detritus, the raw material for decomposition. The important *steps* are: fragmentation, in which detritivores such as the earthworm break detritus down into smaller particles; leaching, in which water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts; catabolism, in which bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances; humification, which leads to the accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous substance called humus that is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes extremely slowly, and being colloidal in nature serves as a reservoir of nutrients; and mineralisation, in which humus is further degraded by some microbes and inorganic nutrients are released. Earthworm is called the farmer's friend because it breaks down complex organic matter and loosens the soil.

points.en: Detritus: dead leaves, bark, flowers, dead animals, faecal matter
Humification → humus: dark, amorphous, colloidal, resistant, nutrient reservoir

narration.en: Decomposition turns detritus into carbon dioxide, water and nutrients in steps: fragmentation by detritivores like earthworms, leaching of soluble nutrients, catabolism by microbial enzymes, humification into humus, and mineralisation that releases inorganic nutrients.

Humification gives humus: dark, amorphous, colloidal, resistant, nutrient reservoir.
Mineralisation: humus gives inorganic nutrients.
Decomposers break down detritus: dead leaves, bark, flowers, dead animals and faecal matter. First, detritivores like earthworms break it into small pieces.
Water-soluble nutrients sink into the soil and settle as salts: leaching. Bacterial and fungal enzymes then break the detritus into simpler substances: catabolism.
Humification makes humus, dark, colloidal and very slow to decompose: a reservoir of nutrients. Microbes slowly mineralise it, releasing inorganic nutrients.
The rate varies. Nitrogen-rich, sugary detritus in warm, moist soil vanishes fast; lignin- and chitin-rich detritus in cold or waterlogged soil lasts long.

narration.en: A fallen leaf goes through five steps before its nutrients return to the soil. Put them in order.

prompt.en: Arrange the steps of decomposition of a fallen leaf.

steps.en: Fragmentation: earthworms and other detritivores break the leaf into small pieces
Leaching: water-soluble inorganic nutrients seep down into the soil
Catabolism: bacterial and fungal enzymes break detritus into simpler inorganic substances
Humification: a dark, amorphous, colloidal humus builds up
Mineralisation: humus is slowly broken down by microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients

explanation.en: Fragmentation by detritivores comes first, then leaching of soluble nutrients and catabolism by bacterial and fungal enzymes. Humification gives humus, which is then slowly mineralised to release inorganic nutrients. In nature all the steps go on at the same time on different bits of detritus; this is their logical sequence.

body.en: *Decomposition* is largely an oxygen-requiring process. Its rate is controlled by the chemical composition of detritus and by climatic factors. In a particular climatic condition, the decomposition rate is slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and quicker if detritus is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars. Temperature and soil moisture are the most important climatic factors, regulating decomposition through their effects on the activities of soil microbes. Warm and moist environments favour decomposition, whereas low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it, resulting in the build-up of organic materials.

points.en: Slow: detritus rich in lignin and chitin
Fast: detritus rich in nitrogen and sugars
Warm and moist favours; cold and anaerobic conditions inhibit

narration.en: Decomposition is fast when detritus is rich in nitrogen and sugars and when it is warm and moist. It is slow for lignin- and chitin-rich detritus, and in cold or oxygen-poor conditions, where organic matter piles up.

problem.en: Predict which decomposes fastest and which slowest: (A) fallen leaves of a legume in a warm, humid Western Ghats forest; (B) woody twigs in the same forest; (C) legume leaves buried in a waterlogged, cold Himalayan bog.

steps.en: A: nitrogen-rich detritus in warm, moist, aerated conditions: fastest.
B: wood is rich in lignin, so it decomposes more slowly than A.
C: low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit decomposition, so organic matter builds up: slowest.
